title: Our father, our king
hook: a litany of requests in the Days of Awe
carry: we have no king but you

segments.voice: Yesterday, Unetaneh Tokef: who by fire, who by water, and the three things that soften the decree. Your line was teshuvah, tefillah, tzedakah. Which one did you do? Today, two words that sit side by side. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

A drought in the land of Israel, nearly two thousand years ago. A public fast is called. A great sage stands before the ark and says the long, proper prayers, blessing after blessing. No rain. Then his student steps up. He doesn't say a long prayer. He says a few short lines, each beginning with the same two words, words that don't quite fit together. And the Talmud says: the rain came down.
screen: `A DROUGHT, A PUBLIC FAST.` → `THE LONG PRAYERS: NO RAIN.` → `TWO WORDS THAT DON'T FIT.`

segments.voice: The sage was Rabbi Eliezer. The student was Rabbi Akiva. And the two words were avinu malkeinu: our father, our king. The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, gives his words: our father, our king, we have no king but you. Our father, our king, for your sake, have mercy on us. That was the seed. Over the centuries, more lines were added, until the prayer became a long litany, in the Ashkenazi rite more than forty lines, each starting the same way. Our father, our king, inscribe us in the book of good life. Our father, our king, renew for us a good year. Our father, our king, hear our voice. It's said during the ten Days of Awe, from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, and on public fast days. But why those two words together? A father is close. You can climb into his lap. A king is far. You approach him with care, and he can judge you. The prayer refuses to choose. God is both: the one who loves you like a parent and the one who holds you to account like a ruler. Some people find the father easier to pray to; some find the king. The prayer makes you hold both in the same breath, line after line. And then the last line, which many congregations sing slowly, together: our father, our king, be gracious to us and answer us, for we have no deeds; deal with us in righteousness and kindness, and save us. After all the requests, an admission: we don't have enough to show. Answer us anyway.
screen: `RABBI AKIVA IN A DROUGHT.` · `A LITANY OF REQUESTS.` · `CLOSE AS A FATHER, FAR AS A KING.` · `WE HAVE NO DEEDS; ANSWER US.` · then, large: `OUR FATHER, OUR KING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it once, slowly. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say the two words, avinu malkeinu, or in English, our father, our king, once, very slowly. Feel the first word come close. Feel the second step back. If prayer isn't yours, think of someone in your life who was both tender and demanding with you: a parent, a coach, a teacher. Hold both sides of them at once. The bell holds the time.
Avinu malkeinu. Our father, our king. Rabbi Akiva's words in a drought, grown into the litany of the Days of Awe.
Your line: we have no king but you. Today, notice when you're being both close and firm with someone, and let both be love. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Avinu Malkeinu is said after the Amidah during the Ten Days of Repentance, from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, and on public fast days, usually with the ark open; it is generally omitted on Shabbat, and its last line is often sung together.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of requests for the new year.
what it means: a prayer that holds God as close as a parent and as high as a ruler, at once.
what a scholar hears: Taanit 25b's Akiva in a drought, grown to about forty-four lines in the Ashkenazi rite, with differing Sephardi versions.

notes: Taanit 25b: Rabbi Eliezer's 24 blessings, then Rabbi Akiva's 'avinu malkeinu' lines; 'nearly two thousand years ago' approximates the early 2nd century; confirm.
Line count in the Ashkenazi rite (about 44) varies by edition; Sephardi versions shorter/different.
Omission on Shabbat (except Neilah in some rites) given generally in howItsDone.
